claim: AgRP neurons distribute neuroendocrine information to other brain regions such as the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH).
source: Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus respond to multiple metabolic signals and distribute neuroendocrine information to other brain regions such as the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH), which plays a central role in metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established scientific knowledge about AgRP neuron function.

claim: Neural projections from AgRP neurons to the PVH form during the postnatal lactational period in mice.
source: Neural projections from AgRP neurons to the PVH form during the postnatal lactational period in mice
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Bouret et al., 2004a).

claim: AgRP projections to the PVH are reduced in offspring of dams that consumed a high-fat diet during lactation (MHFD-L).
source: these projections are reduced in offspring of dams that consumed a high-fat diet (HFD) during lactation (MHFD-L).
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 1K and citations to prior work (Vogt et al., 2014).

claim: MHFD-L exposure causes morphological changes to microglia that are regionally localized to the PVH.
source: we used immunohistochemistry to visualize microglial morphology in MHFD-L offspring and identified changes that were regionally localized to the PVH
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 showing morphological changes in PVH but not in ARH (Figure 2) or BST (Figure 3).

claim: Morphological changes to microglia in the PVH appear temporally restricted to the period when AgRP neurons innervate this region.
source: identified changes that were regionally localized to the PVH and appeared temporally restricted to the period when AgRP neurons innervate this region.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing changes at P16 but not P30 (Figure 1).

claim: Microglia engulf AgRP terminals in the PVH.
source: axon labeling experiments revealed that microglia engulf AgRP terminals in the PVH
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figure 5 showing internalized AgRP terminals within microglia.

claim: The density of AgRP innervation to the PVH in MHFD-L offspring is dependent on microglia.
source: the density of AgRP innervation to the PVH in MHFD-L offspring may be dependent on microglia, because microglial depletion blocked the decrease in PVH AgRP innervation observed in MHFD-L offspring
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PLX5622 microglial depletion experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Microglial depletion prevented the increased body weight exhibited at weaning in MHFD-L offspring.
source: microglial depletion blocked the decrease in PVH AgRP innervation observed in MHFD-L offspring, as well as prevented the increased body weight exhibited at weaning.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4J showing that PLX5622 treatment prevented weight gain in MHFD-L offspring.

claim: Microglia are activated by exposure to MHFD-L.
source: these findings suggest that microglia are activated by exposure to MHFD-L
evidence: The claim is inferred from morphological changes in microglia (increased process complexity, length, territory, and volume) shown in Figure 1, which are consistent with microglial activation.

claim: Microglia interact directly with AgRP axons during postnatal development to permanently alter innervation of the PVH.
source: these findings suggest that microglia are activated by exposure to MHFD-L and interact directly with AgRP axons during postnatal development to permanently alter innervation of the PVH
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing microglial engulfment of AgRP terminals (Figure 5) and the persistent reduction in AgRP innervation at P30 (Figure 1K).

claim: Children born to obese mothers experience higher rates of obesity later in life.
source: Children born to obese mothers experience higher rates of obesity later in life, with accompanying comorbidities that negatively impact health and longevity (Stettler et al., 2005; Whitlock et al., 2009; Tamashiro and Moran, 2010; Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Developmental programming of metabolic phenotype has been reproduced in several animal models.
source: Although this developmental programming of metabolic phenotype has been reproduced in several animal models (Samuelsson et al., 2008; Masuyama and Hiramatsu, 2014; García-Cáceres et al., 2019; Skowronski et al., 2024), the underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Maternal obesity during lactation is particularly impactful on offspring metabolic phenotype in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, maternal obesity during lactation, a time when offspring are dependent on milk from their mothers for nutrition, appears to be particularly impactful.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gorski et al., 2006; Vogt et al., 2014; Calvo-Lerma et al., 2022; Bolton et al., 2022; Skowronski et al., 2024).

claim: Changes to metabolic phenotype from maternal obesity during lactation are thought to be mediated by changes in the milk.
source: These changes to metabolic phenotype are thought to be mediated by changes in the milk (Gorski et al., 2006; Vogt et al., 2014; Calvo-Lerma et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural circuits known to control body weight develop during the lactational period.
source: Because neural circuits known to control body weight develop during the lactational period, they are vulnerable to a variety of environmental signals that may affect their organization and function (Horvath et al., 2010; Bouret et al., 2015; Elson and Simerly, 2015; Zeltser, 2018; Skowronski et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AgRP neurons function as 'hunger neurons'.
source: AgRP neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH) function as 'hunger neurons'
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: AgRP axons extend from the ARH at postnatal day 4 (P4) and reach the PVH between P8-P10.
source: During development, AgRP axons extend from the ARH at postnatal day 4 (P4) and reach the PVH between P8-P10.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Bouret et al., 2004a).

claim: Leptin is required for normal targeting of AgRP axons to downstream regions.
source: Leptin is required for normal targeting of AgRP axons to downstream regions, and in leptin-deficient mice both neuroanatomical and related physiological defects persist into adulthood (Bouret et al., 2004b; Bouyer and Simerly, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Maternal overnutrition affects formation of feeding circuits during postnatal life with concomitant dysregulation of body weight.
source: Maternal overnutrition affects formation of feeding circuits during postnatal life with concomitant dysregulation of body weight (Plagemann et al., 1992; Lippert and Brüning, 2022; Skowronski et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MHFD-L causes suppression of neural projections from AgRP neurons to the PVH in offspring and is associated with increased body weight later in life.
source: Limiting HFD exposure of dams to the first 3 weeks of lactation (MHFD-L) causes suppression of neural projections from AgRP neurons to the PVH in offspring and is associated with increased body weight later in life (Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MHFD-L was more effective than prenatal maternal HFD exposure in causing body weight changes in adult offspring.
source: In fact, MHFD-L was more effective than prenatal maternal HFD exposure in causing body weight changes in adult offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Vogt et al., 2014).

claim: MHFD-L did not alter cell number, peptidergic expression, or cellular activity of AgRP neurons in the ARH.
source: MHFD-L did not alter cell number, peptidergic expression, or cellular activity of AgRP neurons in the ARH
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Vogt et al., 2014) and confirmed by data in Figure 2J.

claim: The effects of both leptin and MHFD-L on targeting AgRP projections display considerable regional specificity.
source: Notably, the effects of both leptin (Kamitakahara et al., 2018) and MHFD-L (Vogt et al., 2014) on targeting AgRP projections display considerable regional specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult mice placed on HFD display a marked hypothalamic gliosis that reveals an acute inflammatory response, which presages significant weight gain.
source: Adult mice placed on HFD display a marked hypothalamic gliosis that reveals an acute inflammatory response, which presages significant weight gain (Horvath et al., 2010; Valdearcos et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2019; Cansell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hypothalamic neuroinflammation is characterized by marked changes in the density and morphology of microglia that are most pronounced in the ARH.
source: This hypothalamic neuroinflammation is characterized by marked changes in the density and morphology of microglia that are most pronounced in the ARH (Thaler et al., 2012; Valdearcos et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia are the resident myeloid cells of the CNS.
source: Microglia are the resident myeloid cells of the CNS
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Microglia respond to a broad array of circulating signals, including nutrients such as saturated fats and carbohydrates.
source: Microglia are the resident myeloid cells of the CNS and respond to a broad array of circulating signals, including nutrients such as saturated fats and carbohydrates (Valdearcos et al., 2014; Nadjar et al., 2017; Leyrolle et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activation of microglia alone is sufficient to stimulate food intake and promote weight gain in adult mice.
source: Moreover, activation of microglia alone is sufficient to stimulate food intake and promote weight gain in adult mice, and perturbations that block activation of microglia reduce the metabolic disruption associated with neuroinflammation (Valdearcos et al., 2017; Rosin and Kurrasch, 2019; Sun et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia have been proposed as possible mediators of developmental programming caused by nutritional perturbations.
source: Because of their established role as nutrient-sensing sentinels of hypothalamic neuroinflammation, and their documented participation in neural development (Stevens et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 2012; Stephan et al., 2012), microglia have been proposed as possible mediators of developmental programming caused by nutritional perturbations (Rosin and Kurrasch, 2019; Folick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia have multiple roles in brain development.
source: Evidence from several lines of investigation indicates that microglia have multiple roles in brain development (Bilbo and Schwarz, 2009; Tremblay et al., 2011; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In vivo imaging experiments demonstrated continual activity of microglial cellular processes, which actively survey their local environment.
source: Although microglia were initially thought to remain quiescent until activation by neuroinflammation, in vivo imaging experiments demonstrated continual activity of their cellular processes, which actively survey their local environment (Nakajima and Kohsaka, 2001; Town et al., 2005; Wake et al., 2009; Stowell et al., 2018), including direct contact with axons and dendrites (Schafer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia are thought to play an important role in synaptic refinement through selective elimination of synapses, a process termed synaptic pruning.
source: In addition to impacting neuronal number and initial formation of neural circuits through effects on axon targeting, microglia are thought to play an important role in synaptic refinement through selective elimination of synapses, a process termed synaptic pruning (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Schafer et al., 2012; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transcriptional profiling suggests a great deal of regional and temporal variation in microglial cell type and activity.
source: However, transcriptional profiling suggests a great deal of regional and temporal variation in microglial cell type and activity (Hammond et al., 2019; Masuda et al., 2020; Young et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the PVH, the overall size of microglia was significantly enhanced in offspring exposed to MHFD-L than those raised on NCD at P16.
source: We found that in the PVH, the overall size of microglia was significantly enhanced in offspring exposed to MHFD-L than those raised on NCD at P16 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: MHFD-L offspring showed a 44% increase in the complexity of microglial process branching in the PVH at P16.
source: The increased size of microglia observed in MHFD-L offspring is demonstrated through a 44% increase in the complexity of microglial process branching, as determined by Sholl analysis (Figure 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: MHFD-L offspring showed an 87% increase in microglial process length in the PVH at P16.
source: as well as an 87% increase in microglial process length (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The volume of microglial cells in the PVH was nearly doubled in MHFD-L offspring at P16.
source: Additionally, the volume of microglial cells (volume measurements include cell body and processes; Figure 1I), and the spatial territory they occupy (Figure 1H), was nearly doubled in MHFD-L offspring
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The density of microglia in the PVH between the dietary groups remained unaltered at P16.
source: while the density of microglia between the dietary groups remained unaltered at P16 (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: By P30, there were no detectable changes in microglial size, cell territory, cell volume, or density between MHFD-L and NCD offspring in the PVH.
source: The changes in microglia between NCD and MHFD-L mice at P16 (Figure 1B and C) appeared to be transient, because by P30 (Figure 1D and E), we did not detect changes in microglial size (process complexity, Figure 1F; and length, Figure 1G), microglia cell territory (Figure 1H), microglial cell volume (Figure 1I), or density of microglial cells (Figure 1J) between MHFD-L and NCD offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 1D-J.

claim: The density of microglia in the PVH was reduced from P16 to P30, independent of dietary treatment.
source: The density of microglia in the PVH was reduced from P16 to P30, although this was independent of dietary treatment (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: AgRP terminal density is significantly lower in the brains of MHFD-L offspring compared with NCD controls at both P16 and P30.
source: The results confirmed that AgRP terminal density is significantly lower in the brains of MHFD-L offspring compared with NCD controls at both P16 and P30 (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Microglial size and density in the ARH were not significantly different in NCD and MHFD-L offspring at P16.
source: In contrast to our findings in the PVH, microglial size and density in the ARH were not significantly different in NCD and MHFD-L offspring at P16 (Figure 2A and B; quantified in 2E-I).

claim: By P30, there was a 67% increase in process length in the ARH of NCD mice compared to their P16 counterparts.
source: By P30 (Figure 2C and D) there was a 67% increase in process length (Figure 2F) of NCD mice compared to their P16 counterparts
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No significant differences in microglial morphology in the ARH were detected between the dietary treatment groups at P30.
source: but no significant differences in microglial morphology in the ARH were detected between the dietary treatment groups (Figure 2A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 2A-G.

claim: The volume of individual microglial cells in the ARH increased from P16 to P30.
source: The volume of individual microglial cells (Figure 2H), as well as the spatial territory they occupy (Figure 2G), increased from P16 to P30
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The total number of microglial cells in the ARH was reduced by nearly half from P16 to P30.
source: while the total number of microglial cells was reduced by nearly half (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The number of AgRP neurons in the ARH is resistant to MHFD-L exposure at both P16 and P30.
source: We also measured numbers of AgRP neuronal cell bodies in the ARH in brains derived from NCD and MHFD-L offspring and confirmed that the number of AgRP neurons in the ARH is also resistant to MHFD-L exposure at both P16 and P30 (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Neither the size nor number of microglia in the BST were significantly different between NCD and MHFD-L offspring at P16 or P30.
source: As was found for the ARH, neither the size nor number of microglia in the BST were significantly different between NCD and MHFD-L offspring at P16 or P30 (Figure 3A–D; quantified in 3E-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 3A-I.

claim: The density of AgRP terminals in the BST was not affected by MHFD-L exposure.
source: Similarly, the density of AgRP terminals in the same region of interest was not affected by MHFD-L exposure (Figure 3J)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: By P30, the number of AgRP terminals in the BST increased by 61% compared to their P16 counterparts.
source: although by P30 the number of AgRP terminals in the BST increased by 61% compared to their P16 counterparts (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: PLX5622 treatments from P4-P21 resulted in a significant decrease in microglia detected in the hypothalamus at P55 relative to age-matched controls.
source: These postnatal treatments resulted in a significant decrease in microglia detected in the hypothalamus at P55 relative to age-matched controls (Figure 4B and C; quantified in 4 H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 4B, C, and H.

claim: PLX5622 treatments blocked the reduction in AgRP fiber density observed in the PVHmpd of vehicle-treated MHFD-L offspring.
source: Notably, the PLX5622 treatments blocked the reduction in AgRP fiber density observed in the medial dorsal parvicellular part of the PVH (PVHmpd) of vehicle-treated MHFD-L offspring to a level that was comparable to that of NCD offspring (Figure 4D–G; quantified in 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 4D-G and I.

claim: MHFD-L exposure did not affect the density of AgRP fibers in the PVHpml.
source: In contrast, MHFD-L exposure did not affect the density of AgRP fibers in the lateral posterior magnocellular compartment of the PVH (PVHpml) and no significant difference in AgRP fiber density was detected between NCD and MHFD-L offspring treated with either PLX5622 or vehicle (Figure 4D–G; quantified in 4 K)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 4D-G and K.

claim: The body weight of vehicle-treated MHFD-L animals was significantly greater (24%) compared with that of NCD animals at weaning.
source: In keeping with previously published results (Vogt et al., 2014), the body weight of vehicle-treated MHFD-L animals was significantly greater (24%), compared with that of NCD animals at weaning (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J and citation to prior research.

claim: MHFD-L mice treated with PLX5622 during lactation exhibited significantly lower weights at weaning compared to those of vehicle-treated MHFD-L animals.
source: However, MHFD-L mice treated with PLX5622 during lactation exhibited significantly lower weights at weaning compared to those of vehicle-treated MHFD-L animals (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Many apparent contacts between microglial processes and AgRP terminals in the PVH and ARH were observed at P16 and P30, including internalized AgRP terminals.
source: Many apparent contacts between microglial processes and AgRP terminals in the PVH and ARH were observed at P16 and P30, including internalized AgRP terminals (Figure 5A–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 5A-L.

claim: The extent of internalization of AgRP terminals did not appear to be influenced by MHFD-L exposure.
source: However, the extent of internalization did not appear to be influenced by MHFD-L exposure; there were no significant differences between internalized AgRP terminals in MHFD-L and NCD offspring at P16, in either the PVH or ARH (Figure 5M and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 5M and O.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in microglial CD68 levels in the PVH between diet groups at either P16 or P30.
source: Similarly, we did not detect a statistically significant difference in microglial CD68 levels in the PVH between diet groups at either P16 or P30 (Figure 5N).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: The density of CD68 labeled profiles nearly doubled in the PVH between P16 and P30.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Wong et al., 2005; Hart et al., 2012), the density of CD68 labeled profiles nearly doubled in the PVH between P16 and P30 (Figure 5N), as microglia become more phagocytic with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5N and citations to prior research.

claim: In the ARH, CD68 staining increased between P16 and P30.
source: In the ARH, CD68 staining also increased between P16 and P30 (Figure 5P), supporting the notion that microglia increase their phagocytic capacity with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5P.

claim: Microglia interact directly with AgRP terminals, with clear evidence of engulfment.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis demonstrates that microglia interact directly with AgRP terminals, with clear evidence of engulfment.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MHFD-L exposure does not appear to promote microglia-mediated engulfment of AgRP terminals in the PVH and ARH.
source: MHFD-L exposure does not appear to promote microglia-mediated engulfment, at least not in the specific PVH and ARH domains examined.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of significant differences in engulfment between MHFD-L and NCD groups shown in Figures 5M and O.

claim: Microglia are required for significant elevations in body weight that emerge from postnatal exposure to HFD.
source: Here, we demonstrate that microglia are required for significant elevations in body weight that emerge from postnatal exposure to HFD and are associated with a sustained decrease in the density of afferents from AgRP neurons to the PVH in offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from PLX5622 depletion experiments shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Exposure to MHFD-L caused distinct morphological changes to microglia that were observed in the PVH, but not the ARH or BST.
source: Exposure to MHFD-L caused distinct morphological changes to microglia that may be consistent with enhanced activity, which were observed in the PVH, but not the ARH or BST.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The morphological changes to microglia observed appear to be primarily limited to the critical period for the development of AgRP inputs to PVH neurons in MHFD-L offspring.
source: Moreover, the morphological changes to microglia observed appear to be primarily limited to the critical period for the development of AgRP inputs to PVH neurons in MHFD-L offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing changes at P16 but not P30 (Figure 1).

claim: Microglia engage in engulfment of AgRP terminals in the PVH during development.
source: Although our results demonstrate that microglia engage in engulfment of AgRP terminals in the PVH during development
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Synaptic pruning by microglia does not appear to represent the cellular mechanism mediating the effects of MHFD-L exposure on innervation of the PVH by AgRP neurons.
source: synaptic pruning by microglia does not appear to represent the cellular mechanism mediating the effects of MHFD-L exposure on innervation of the PVH by AgRP neurons.

claim: Maternal HFD exposure during perinatal development leads to increased body weight, fat content, and susceptibility to diet-induced obesity in offspring.
source: Maternal HFD exposure during perinatal development leads to increased body weight, fat content, and susceptibility to diet-induced obesity in offspring (Samuelsson et al., 2008; Tamashiro et al., 2009; Masuyama and Hiramatsu, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The postnatal period is especially sensitive to nutritional environment and exposure to HFD that is exclusive to this period plays a particularly dominant role in specifying metabolic phenotype later in life.
source: The postnatal period, which corresponds to lactation, and when mice derive their nutrition primarily from milk, is especially sensitive to nutritional environment and exposure to HFD that is exclusive to this period plays a particularly dominant role in specifying metabolic phenotype later in life (Chen et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2024; Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Global depletion of microglia with the CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 blocked the ability of MHFD-L to increase body weight in mice by weaning at P21.
source: In the present study, global depletion of microglia with the CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 blocked the ability of MHFD-L to increase body weight in mice by weaning at P21, indicating microglia may mediate metabolic changes caused by MHFD-L exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Microglial depletion with PLX5622 in adult mice mitigates the effects of HFD exposure.
source: Consistent with this, microglial depletion with PLX5622 in adult mice mitigates the effects of HFD exposure (Rosin and Kurrasch, 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MHFD-L exposure caused a marked increase in the overall size of microglia in the PVH that is related to increases in both the length and branching complexity of immunolabeled Iba1 cellular processes.
source: In our studies, MHFD-L exposure caused a marked increase in the overall size of microglia in the PVH that is related to increases in both the length and branching complexity of immunolabeled Iba1 cellular processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The increase in the territory occupied by microglia in the PVH was not accompanied by an increase in microglial number.
source: This increase in the territory occupied by microglia in the PVH was not accompanied by an increase in microglial number, nor were numbers of microglia affected in the PVH by MHFD-L exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Changes in microglial morphology were not observed in the ARH in response to MHFD-L.
source: However, in contrast to the PVH, changes in microglial morphology were not observed in the ARH in response to MHFD-L

claim: An overall increase in process length in the ARH was observed between P16 and P30 of both MHFD-L and NCD mice.
source: although we did observe an overall increase in process length in the ARH between P16 and P30 of both MHFD-L and NCD mice.

claim: Comparable changes in microglial morphology were not observed in the BST.
source: As in the ARH, we did not observe comparable changes in microglial morphology in the BST, an extrahypothalamic target of AgRP neurons innervated during the lactation period (Cansell et al., 2012; Barbier et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior research.

claim: The observed morphological changes in the PVH caused by MHFD-L appear to be transient as there are no significant differences in microglial processes by P30.
source: Moreover, the observed morphological changes in the PVH caused by MHFD-L appear to be transient as there are no significant differences in microglial processes by P30
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F-I.

claim: The density of microglial cells in the PVH was significantly reduced in the older mice (P30 compared to P16), suggesting a decline in overall activity.
source: and the density of microglial cells in the PVH was significantly reduced in the older mice, suggesting a decline in overall activity.

claim: The partial rescue of innervation by PLX5622 appeared to be limited to the PVHmpd, suggesting regional specialization in the activity of microglia in the PVH.

claim: No change in AgRP innervation of the BST was observed in MHFD-L offspring that mirrored the changes seen in the PVH of the same animals.
source: We did not observe a change in AgRP innervation of the BST in MHFD-L offspring that mirrored the changes seen in the PVH of the same animals

claim: Microglia display at least some degree of spatial heterogeneity in mediating site-specific alterations in AgRP axon targeting.
source: further supporting the conclusion that microglia display at least some degree of spatial heterogeneity in mediating site-specific alterations in AgRP axon targeting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects observed in PVH versus BST and ARH.

claim: Microglia are known to impact a variety of developmental events, including alterations in cell number through programmed cell death or neurogenesis, as well as axonal targeting and remodeling of neural circuits.
source: Microglia are known to impact a variety of developmental events, including alterations in cell number through programmed cell death or neurogenesis, as well as axonal targeting and remodeling of neural circuits (Frost and Schafer, 2016; Li and Barres, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is unlikely that the impaired innervation of the PVH observed in MHFD-L offspring is due to a reduction in the number of AgRP neurons in the ARH.
source: It is unlikely that the impaired innervation of the PVH observed in MHFD-L offspring is due to a reduction in the number of AgRP neurons in the ARH (Vogt et al., 2014; Valdearcos et al., 2017).

claim: Microglial depletion during postnatal life increases numbers of NPY neurons and enhances local densities of AgRP fibers in the ARH.
source: Sun et al., 2024 reported that microglial depletion during postnatal life increases numbers of NPY neurons, as well as enhances local densities of AgRP fibers in the ARH, possibly through enhanced formation of perineuronal nets.

claim: Depletion of microglia during gestation causes a significant decrease in the number of POMC neurons in the ARH and leads to an acceleration of weight gain.
